title: The dative: likes, gifts, birthdays and dates
objectives: I can form the dative singular of nouns, adjectives and possessives, and say to whom I give, tell or buy something.
I can use the dative pronouns 'мені́', 'тобі́', 'йому́', 'їй', 'нам', 'вам' and 'їм', and tell them apart from the accusative forms 'мене́', 'тебе́', 'його́'.
I can say what I like with 'подо́батися', making the verb agree with the thing liked, and say what someone needs or may do with 'тре́ба' and 'мо́жна'.
I can name the months, ask and give the date, and say on which date or in which month something happens.
I can explain why 'по́друга' becomes 'по́друзі', why 'сі́чень' loses its 'е' in 'сі́чня', and why 'лю́тий' takes adjective endings.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'сі́чня', locative 'у сі́чні'. The names of the months are written with a small letter.

example.target: У сі́чні в Ки́єві ду́же хо́лодно.
example.source: In January it is very cold in Kyiv.
example.source_literal: In January in Kyiv very cold.

vocabulary.part_of_speech: masculine noun, declined like an adjective
vocabulary.note: The name is the adjective 'лю́тий', fierce or bitter, used as a noun for the month of hard frosts. As a former adjective it keeps adjective endings: genitive 'лю́того', locative 'у лю́тому'.

example.target: У ме́не день наро́дження в лю́тому.
example.source: My birthday is in February.
example.source_literal: At me day of-birth in February.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'бе́резня', locative 'у бе́резні'. The name comes from 'бере́за', birch.

example.target: Два́дцять дру́гого бе́резня в Оле́ни день наро́дження.
example.source: Olena's birthday is on March twenty-second.
example.source_literal: Twenty of-second of-March at Olena day of-birth.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'кві́тня', locative 'у кві́тні'. The name comes from 'квіт', blossom.

example.target: У кві́тні вже те́пло.
example.source: In April it is already warm.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'тра́вня', locative 'у тра́вні'. The name comes from 'трава́', grass.

example.target: У тра́вні ми бу́демо гуля́ти в па́рку.
example.source: In May we will go for walks in the park.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'че́рвня', locative 'у че́рвні'.

example.target: У че́рвні в Окса́ни бу́дуть кані́кули.
example.source: Oksana will be on break in June.
example.source_literal: In June at Oksana will-be break.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'ли́пня', locative 'у ли́пні'. The name comes from 'ли́па', the linden tree, which flowers in this month.

example.target: У ли́пні ми бу́демо відпочива́ти на мо́рі.
example.source: In July we will be on vacation at the sea.
example.source_literal: In July we will-be to-rest on sea.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'се́рпня', locative 'у се́рпні'. The name comes from 'серп', sickle, the tool of the harvest.

example.target: Два́дцять четве́ртого се́рпня в Украї́ні свя́то.
example.source: On August twenty-fourth there is a holiday in Ukraine.
example.source_literal: Twenty of-fourth of-August in Ukraine holiday.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'ве́ресня', locative 'у ве́ресні'. The name comes from 'ве́рес', heather, which flowers in this month.

example.target: Пе́ршого ве́ресня ді́ти йдуть до шко́ли.
example.source: On September first children go to school.
example.source_literal: Of-first of-September children go to school.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'жо́втня', locative 'у жо́втні'. The name comes from 'жо́втий', yellow, the color of the leaves.

example.target: У жо́втні Тара́с був у Льво́ві.
example.source: In October Taras was in Lviv.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'листопа́да', locative 'у листопа́ді'. The name joins 'лист', leaf, and the verb 'па́дати', to fall.

example.target: Сього́дні дев’я́те листопа́да.
example.source: Today is November ninth.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'гру́дня', locative 'у гру́дні'. The name comes from 'гру́да', a frozen lump of earth.

example.target: Два́дцять п’я́того гру́дня в Украї́ні Різдво́.
example.source: On December twenty-fifth Ukraine celebrates Christmas.
example.source_literal: Twenty of-fifth of-December in Ukraine Christmas.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'мі́сяця'. One word names both the month and the moon, because the old calendar counted months by the moon.

example.target: Насту́пного мі́сяця я бу́ду в Оде́сі.
example.source: Next month I will be in Odesa.
example.source_literal: Of-next of-month I will-be in Odesa.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'числа́', plural 'чи́сла', with the stress moving. In a date the ordinal numeral agrees with 'число́', so it is neuter: 'пе́рше', 'дру́ге'.

example.target: Яке́ сього́дні число́?
example.source: What is the date today?

vocabulary.source: to be liked by, to please
vocabulary.note: Perfective 'сподо́батися'. The thing liked is the subject and the person who likes it is in the dative, so the verb agrees with the thing: 'подо́бається' for one, 'подо́баються' for several.

example.target: Мені́ подо́бається ця пі́сня.
example.source: I like this song.

vocabulary.note: Present 'дару́ю', 'дару́єш'; perfective 'подарува́ти', future 'подару́ю', 'подару́єш'. The gift is in the accusative and the person who receives it in the dative.

example.target: Ми завжди́ дару́ємо ма́мі кни́ги.
example.source: We always give Mom books.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'пода́рунка', with the 'о' of the last syllable dropping out. It comes from 'дарува́ти'.

example.target: Це пода́рунок для тебе́.
example.source: This is a present for you.

vocabulary.note: 'Наро́дження', birth, is a neuter noun in the genitive here, with the same spelling as its nominative. The greeting is 'З днем наро́дження!', literally 'with day of-birth', where 'днем' is a form of 'день' in the instrumental case, the subject of the next unit.

example.target: Коли́ твій день наро́дження?
example.source: When is your birthday?

vocabulary.note: Perfective 'допомогти́', future 'допоможу́', 'допомо́жеш', past 'допомі́г', 'допомогла́'. The person helped is in the dative, where English uses a direct object.

example.target: Тара́с ча́сто допомага́є ма́мі.
example.source: Taras often helps his mom.

vocabulary.source: it is necessary, one needs to
vocabulary.note: It is the whole predicate of a sentence without a subject, followed by an infinitive. The person who needs to act is in the dative.

example.target: Мені́ тре́ба купи́ти хліб.
example.source: I need to buy bread.

dialogues.title: A present for Olena
dialogues.context: Oksana and Taras are at Andrii's café. Taras's sister Olena has a birthday soon, and the two friends, who say 'ти' to each other, choose a present for her.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Тара́се, коли́ в Оле́ни день наро́дження?
lines.source: Taras, when is Olena's birthday?
lines.source_literal: Taras, when at Olena day of-birth?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: У субо́ту, два́дцять дру́гого бе́резня.
lines.source: On Saturday, March twenty-second.
lines.source_literal: On Saturday, twenty of-second of-March.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Це незаба́ром! Скі́льки їй бу́де ро́ків?
lines.source: That's soon! How old will she be?
lines.source_literal: This soon! How-many to-her will-be of-years?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Два́дцять ві́сім. Але́ що їй подарува́ти, я не зна́ю.
lines.source: Twenty-eight. But I don't know what to give her.
lines.source_literal: Twenty eight. But what to-her to-give, I not know.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Я тобі́ допоможу́. Що їй подо́бається?
lines.source: I'll help you. What does she like?
lines.source_literal: I to-you will-help. What to-her pleases?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Їй подо́баються кни́ги й украї́нські пі́сні.
lines.source: She likes books and Ukrainian songs.
lines.source_literal: To-her please books and Ukrainian songs.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А мину́лого ро́ку ти подарува́в їй кни́гу?
lines.source: And did you give her a book last year?
lines.source_literal: And of-last of-year you gave to-her book?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Так, і вона́ їй ду́же сподо́балася.
lines.source: Yes, and she liked it very much.
lines.source_literal: Yes, and it to-her very pleased.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Мо́жна подарува́ти їй квитки́ на конце́рт. Вона́ лю́бить конце́рти?
lines.source: We could give her concert tickets. Does she like concerts?
lines.source_literal: Possible to-give to-her tickets to concert. She loves concerts?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ду́же лю́бить! Але́ квитки́ дорогі́.
lines.source: She loves them! But the tickets are expensive.
lines.source_literal: Very loves! But tickets expensive.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ми мо́жемо купи́ти їх ра́зом. Це бу́де наш пода́рунок.
lines.source: We can buy them together. It will be our present.
lines.source_literal: We can to-buy them together. This will-be our present.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: До́бре! Дя́кую тобі́, Окса́но.
lines.source: Great! Thank you, Oksana.
lines.source_literal: Good! I-thank to-you, Oksana.

dialogues.title: A birthday call
dialogues.context: It is Iryna Petrivna's birthday, and Sam phones his teacher. She answers with 'Слу́хаю', literally 'I-listen', a common way to answer the phone. Sam also says 'Бажа́ю вам ща́стя!', I wish you happiness, literally 'I-wish to-you of-happiness': the verb 'бажа́ти', to wish, takes the person in the dative and the thing wished in the genitive. They say 'ви' to each other.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Слу́хаю.
lines.source: Hello?
lines.source_literal: I-listen.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́брий день, Іри́но Петрі́вно! Це Сем. З днем наро́дження!
lines.source: Good afternoon, Iryna Petrivna! It's Sam. Happy birthday!
lines.source_literal: Good day, Iryna Petrivna! This Sam. With day of-birth!

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Се́ме, ду́же дя́кую! А зві́дки ви зна́єте?
lines.source: Sam, thank you very much! But how do you know?
lines.source_literal: Sam, very I-thank! And where-from you know?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Окса́на мені́ сказа́ла. Бажа́ю вам ща́стя!
lines.source: Oksana told me. I wish you happiness!
lines.source_literal: Oksana to-me told. I-wish to-you of-happiness!

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Дя́кую! Мені́ ду́же приє́мно.
lines.source: Thank you! I am very pleased.
lines.source_literal: I-thank! To-me very pleasant.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Іри́но Петрі́вно, а коли́ День Незале́жності? Тара́с запро́шує мене́ в центр на свя́то.
lines.source: Iryna Petrivna, when is Independence Day? Taras is inviting me downtown for the holiday.
lines.source_literal: Iryna Petrivna, and when Day of-Independence? Taras invites me to center for holiday.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Два́дцять четве́ртого се́рпня. Це вели́ке свя́то.
lines.source: On August twenty-fourth. It is a big holiday.
lines.source_literal: Twenty of-fourth of-August. This big holiday.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А яке́ сього́дні число́?
lines.source: And what is the date today?
lines.source_literal: And which today number?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Сього́дні два́дцять дру́ге. Свя́то бу́де че́рез два дні.
lines.source: Today is the twenty-second. The holiday is in two days.
lines.source_literal: Today twenty second. Holiday will-be through two days.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую! За́втра я скажу́ Тара́сові «так».
lines.source: Thank you! Tomorrow I'll tell Taras yes.
lines.source_literal: I-thank! Tomorrow I will-tell to-Taras «yes».

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ду́же до́бре. До поба́чення, Се́ме!
lines.source: Very good. Goodbye, Sam!
lines.source_literal: Very well. Until seeing, Sam!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До поба́чення, Іри́но Петрі́вно!
lines.source: Goodbye, Iryna Petrivna!
lines.source_literal: Until seeing, Iryna Petrivna!

dialogues.title: Andrii helps a customer
dialogues.context: Mariia Ivanivna, a retired neighbor, comes into Andrii's café. She and Andrii say 'ви' to each other; he calls her 'па́ні Марі́є', and she calls him 'па́не Андрі́ю'.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: До́брий день, па́ні Марі́є! Вам ка́ву, як завжди́?
lines.source: Good afternoon, Mariia! Your usual coffee?
lines.source_literal: Good day, Ms. Mariia! To-you coffee, as always?

lines.speaker: Марі́я Іва́нівна
lines.target: Так, дя́кую. Па́не Андрі́ю, ви мені́ допомо́жете?
lines.source: Yes, thank you. Andrii, will you help me?
lines.source_literal: Yes, I-thank. Mr. Andrii, you to-me will-help?

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Звича́йно. Що вам тре́ба?
lines.source: Of course. What do you need?
lines.source_literal: Of-course. What to-you necessary?

lines.speaker: Марі́я Іва́нівна
lines.target: За́втра в мого́ си́на день наро́дження. Мені́ тре́ба купи́ти йому́ пода́рунок.
lines.source: Tomorrow is my son's birthday. I need to buy him a present.
lines.source_literal: Tomorrow at my son day of-birth. To-me necessary to-buy to-him present.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: А що йому́ подо́бається?
lines.source: And what does he like?
lines.source_literal: And what to-him pleases?

lines.speaker: Марі́я Іва́нівна
lines.target: Він ду́же лю́бить ка́ву. А ва́ша ка́ва йому́ ду́же сподо́балася.
lines.source: He loves coffee. And he really liked your coffee.
lines.source_literal: He very loves coffee. And your coffee to-him very pleased.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Мо́жна подарува́ти йому́ на́шу ка́ву. Ось ця ду́же смачна́.
lines.source: You could give him our coffee. This one here is very good.
lines.source_literal: Possible to-give to-him our coffee. Here this very tasty.

lines.speaker: Марі́я Іва́нівна
lines.target: Скі́льки вона́ ко́штує?
lines.source: How much is it?
lines.source_literal: How-much it costs?

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Сто гри́вень. І я дам вам ча́шку для ньо́го. Це мій пода́рунок.
lines.source: A hundred hryvnias. And I'll give you a cup for him. It's my present.
lines.source_literal: Hundred of-hryvnias. And I will-give to-you cup for him. This my present.

lines.speaker: Марі́я Іва́нівна
lines.target: Дя́кую вам! Але́ мій син живе́ у Льво́ві. Що мені́ тре́ба роби́ти?
lines.source: Thank you! But my son lives in Lviv. What do I need to do?
lines.source_literal: I-thank to-you! But my son lives in Lviv. What to-me necessary to-do?

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Вам тре́ба сього́дні йти на по́шту, і за́втра пода́рунок бу́де у Льво́ві.
lines.source: You need to go to the post office today, and tomorrow the present will be in Lviv.
lines.source_literal: To-you necessary today to-go to post-office, and tomorrow present will-be in Lviv.

lines.speaker: Марі́я Іва́нівна
lines.target: А де по́шта? Це дале́ко?
lines.source: And where is the post office? Is it far?
lines.source_literal: And where post-office? This far?

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Ні, це бли́зько. Пря́мо, по́тім ліво́руч.
lines.source: No, it's close. Straight ahead, then left.
lines.source_literal: No, this near. Straight, then on-the-left.

lines.speaker: Марі́я Іва́нівна
lines.target: Дя́кую, па́не Андрі́ю! Ви мені́ ду́же допомогли́.
lines.source: Thank you, Andrii! You've been a great help.
lines.source_literal: I-thank, Mr. Andrii! You to-me very helped.

grammar.title: The dative case: the person who receives
grammar.explanation:
The dative case marks the person who receives something, is told something or gains from an action. Its Ukrainian name, 'дава́льний', comes from 'дава́ти', to give: it is the case of the one to whom something is given. It answers the question 'кому́?' (to whom?) and, for things, 'чому́?' (to what?). This 'чому́' is the dative of 'що'; the word 'чому́' meaning why grew out of it and has the same spelling.

English shows the receiver in one of two ways: with the word 'to' ('I gave the book to Mom') or by word order alone ('I gave Mom the book'). Ukrainian puts an ending on the noun instead. In 'Я дала́ ма́мі кни́гу.' (I gave Mom the book, literally 'I gave to-mom book'), 'ма́мі' is the dative of 'ма́ма' and 'кни́гу' is the accusative, the direct object. Because the endings carry the roles, the words can change places and the meaning stays: 'Кни́гу я дала́ ма́мі.' still says that Mom received the book.

The singular endings depend on gender and on the last letter of the noun:

- Feminine nouns in '-а' or '-я' take '-і': 'ма́ма', 'ма́мі'; 'сестра́', 'сестрі́'; 'бабу́ся', 'бабу́сі'.
- Before this '-і', 'г', 'к' and 'х' change to 'з', 'ц' and 'с', as they do before the locative '-і': 'по́друга', 'по́друзі'; 'ті́тка', 'ті́тці'.
- In a noun in '-ія', 'й' plus '-і' is written 'ї': 'Со́фія', 'Со́фії'.
- Feminine nouns that end in a consonant take '-і' too: 'ніч', 'но́чі'; 'ма́ти', 'ма́тері', on the stem 'ма́тер-' of the genitive.
- Masculine nouns take '-ові' after a hard consonant, '-еві' after a soft one or after 'ж', 'ч', 'ш' and 'щ', and '-єві' after 'й': 'брат', 'бра́тові'; 'вчи́тель', 'вчи́телеві'; 'Андрі́й', 'Андрі́єві'. Masculine nouns in '-о' do the same: 'та́то', 'та́тові'.
- Masculine nouns can also take the shorter '-у' or '-ю': 'бра́ту', 'вчи́телю', 'Андрі́ю'. For people and animals the longer ending is preferred.
- Neuter nouns take '-у' after a hard consonant and '-ю' after a soft one: 'мі́сто', 'мі́сту'; 'мо́ре', 'мо́рю'.

A masculine noun in '-а' that names a man, such as 'Мико́ла', declines like 'ма́ма', so its dative is 'Мико́лі'. It is still masculine, and words that agree with it are masculine.

When a title and a name for one man stand side by side, Ukrainian usually puts '-ові' on the first and '-у' or '-ю' on the second, so that the long ending is not repeated: 'па́нові Андрі́ю', to Andrii, literally 'to-Mr. to-Andrii'.

The stress of the dative is usually the stress of the genitive singular: 'сестри́', 'сестрі́'; 'бра́та', 'бра́тові'; 'мі́ста', 'мі́сту'.

examples.source: I gave my sister the key.
We bought our brother a jacket.
The children are giving their mother a present.

grammar.title: Dative pronouns, adjectives and possessives
grammar.explanation:
The personal pronouns have their own dative forms. Learn them beside the accusative forms from the food unit, because some of them begin alike and are easy to confuse:

- 'мене́', me, and 'мені́', to me
- 'тебе́', you, and 'тобі́', to you
- 'його́', him, and 'йому́', to him
- 'її́', her, and 'їй', to her
- 'нас', us, and 'нам', to us
- 'вас', you, and 'вам', to you
- 'їх', them, and 'їм', to them

'Я ба́чу тебе́.' (I see you) has the accusative, because 'you' is what is seen. 'Я дам тобі́ ключ.' (I will give you the key, literally 'I will-give to-you key') has the dative, because 'you' receives the key. 'Тобі́' has 'о' where 'тебе́' has 'е'. 'Йому́' is the dative of both 'він' and 'воно́'.

A dative pronoun often stands before the verb, which is the most common order in speech: 'Я тобі́ допоможу́.' and 'Я допоможу́ тобі́.' both mean 'I will help you'.

An adjective, a possessive pronoun or a demonstrative before a noun in the dative takes the dative too. There are two endings in the singular:

- '-ому' for masculine and neuter: 'ново́му вчи́телеві', 'моє́му бра́тові', 'на́шому мі́сту', 'цьо́му хло́пцеві'
- '-ій' for feminine: 'нові́й сусі́дці', 'мої́й ма́мі', 'на́шій бабу́сі', 'цій жі́нці'

These are the same endings as in the locative, but the dative has no preposition before it: 'у ново́му мі́сті' is in the new city, while 'ново́му вчи́телеві' is to the new teacher. Soft-stem adjectives write '-ьому': 'си́ньому'. In the dative, 'мій' and 'твій' are 'моє́му' and 'твоє́му', with the stress on 'є'.

'Його́', 'її́' and 'їх' meaning his, her and their never change, because they are genitive forms of 'він', 'вона́' and 'вони́': 'його́ ма́мі', to his mom; 'її́ бра́тові', to her brother.

examples.source: This is a present for the new teacher.

grammar.title: Verbs with a dative: giving, telling, phoning and helping
grammar.explanation:
Many verbs take two objects: the thing, in the accusative, and the person who receives it, in the dative. The verbs of giving, telling and buying for someone work this way:

- 'дава́ти' and 'да́ти', to give
- 'дарува́ти' and 'подарува́ти', to give as a present
- 'каза́ти' and 'сказа́ти', to say, to tell
- 'купува́ти' and 'купи́ти', to buy, here for someone

In 'Тара́с купи́в ма́мі ка́ву.' (Taras bought Mom coffee, literally 'Taras bought to-mom coffee'), 'ка́ву' is what was bought and 'ма́мі' is who gets it. The same meaning can be said with 'для' and the genitive, which you already know: 'Тара́с купи́в ка́ву для ма́ми.'

Some verbs take no direct object at all: the person they are directed at is in the dative, where English uses a direct object. Three common ones are:

- 'дзвони́ти', to phone: the call goes to the person. Its perfective partner is 'подзвони́ти' ('подзвоню́', 'подзво́ниш').
- 'допомага́ти', to help: the help is given to the person. Its perfective partner is 'допомогти́'.
- 'дя́кувати', to thank: the thanks are given to the person. 'Дя́кую' is its 'я' form, so 'Дя́кую тобі́!' is literally 'I-thank to-you!'

So 'I'm phoning Mom' is 'Я дзвоню́ ма́мі.', and 'We help Oksana' is 'Ми допомага́ємо Окса́ні.' Learn these three verbs with the question 'кому́?'.

Aspect works as in the earlier units. 'Я дару́ю ма́мі кни́ги.' is a repeated action, while 'Я подару́ю ма́мі кни́гу.' is one present that will be given. The perfective future of 'допомогти́' is 'допоможу́', 'допомо́жеш', 'допомо́же', and its past is 'допомі́г', 'допомогла́', 'допомогли́'.

examples.source: What did Taras give his sister?
I bought my friend a book.

grammar.title: The person in the dative: liking, needing, feeling and age
grammar.explanation:
In some Ukrainian sentences the person who experiences something is not the subject but stands in the dative. English makes that person the subject: 'I like', 'I need', 'I am cold'. Ukrainian presents the person as the one to whom something happens.

The verb 'подо́батися' means to please. In 'Мені́ подо́бається ця кни́га.' (I like this book) the subject is 'ця кни́га', and the sentence literally says 'to-me pleases this book'. Because the thing liked is the subject, the verb agrees with it:

- one thing: 'Мені́ подо́бається ця кни́га.'
- several things: 'Мені́ подо́баються ці кни́ги.'
- in the past, the gender of the thing: 'подо́бався фільм', 'подо́балася кни́га', 'подо́балося кафе́', 'подо́балися пі́сні'
- an infinitive, with the 'воно́' form: 'Мені́ подо́бається чита́ти.', 'Мені́ подо́балося чита́ти.'

A person who is liked is the subject too: 'Ти мені́ подо́баєшся.' (I like you, literally 'you to-me please'). The perfective 'сподо́батися' names the moment of starting to like something, often the first time: 'Мені́ сподо́бався Львів.' (I liked Lviv). The verb 'люби́ти' takes the person as subject and the thing as a direct object, and it is stronger and lasting: 'Я люблю́ ка́ву.' (I love coffee). 'Подо́батися' is the everyday word for finding something pleasant.

A predicative word is the whole predicate of a sentence without a grammatical subject, as you saw with 'мо́жна', 'те́пло' and 'хо́лодно'. With such a word the person goes in the dative:

- 'Мені́ тре́ба працюва́ти.' (I need to work, literally 'to-me necessary to-work')
- 'Тобі́ мо́жна.' (You may, literally 'to-you possible')
- 'Мені́ хо́лодно.' (I am cold, literally 'to-me cold')
- 'Мені́ ду́же приє́мно.' (I am very pleased, literally 'to-me very pleasant')

Without a dative the sentence is general: 'Сього́дні хо́лодно.' describes the weather, and 'Тре́ба працюва́ти.' means that work must be done. The past adds 'було́' and the future adds 'бу́де': 'Мені́ тре́ба було́ працюва́ти.' (I had to work); 'Нам бу́де хо́лодно.' (We will be cold).

Age uses the same pattern. 'Мені́ два́дцять ро́ків.' (I am twenty) is literally 'to-me twenty of-years': the person whose age is given is in the dative, and the forms 'рік', 'ро́ки' and 'ро́ків' after a number work as in the unit on numbers. The past takes 'було́' and the future 'бу́де': 'Мені́ було́ де́сять ро́ків.' (I was ten); 'Їй бу́де два́дцять ві́сім.' (She will be twenty-eight).

grammar.title: Dates: ordinal numerals and the months
grammar.explanation:
An ordinal numeral puts things in order: 'пе́рший', first; 'дру́гий', second; 'тре́тій', third. Ordinal numerals decline like adjectives and agree with their noun, but they are numerals, not adjectives. You met their feminine forms when telling the time ('пе́рша', 'дру́га'), because they agree with 'годи́на'.

To ask the date, say 'Яке́ сього́дні число́?', literally 'which today number?', meaning 'What is the date today?'. In the answer the word 'число́' is left out, but the ordinal still agrees with it, so it is neuter; the month follows in the genitive, as 'of' the month:

- 'Сього́дні пе́рше тра́вня.' (Today is May first, literally 'today first of-May')
- 'Сього́дні тре́тє ли́пня.' (Today is July third)

To say on which date something happens, the ordinal goes into the genitive as well, with no preposition: 'пе́ршого тра́вня', on May first, literally 'of-first of-May'. The question is 'Коли́?' or 'Яко́го числа́?', literally 'of-which of-number?', meaning 'on what date?', and the answer can be the date alone: 'Двадця́того бе́резня.' (On March twentieth.)

In a compound number only the last word is an ordinal, and only that word changes; the words before it stay cardinal numerals: 'два́дцять пе́рше', 'два́дцять пе́ршого'; 'три́дцять пе́рше'. The ordinals 'двадця́тий' and 'тридця́тий' have the stress on 'я', while the cardinals 'два́дцять' and 'три́дцять' have it on the first syllable.

A month without a date is said with 'у' or 'в' and the locative: 'у тра́вні', in May; 'у лю́тому', in February. The names of the months are masculine nouns written with a small letter. Most end in '-ень' and lose their 'е' in other forms ('сі́чень', 'сі́чня'); 'листопа́д' has the genitive 'листопа́да'; 'лю́тий' declines like an adjective. The next note explains why.

A day of the week and a date can stand together: 'У субо́ту, два́дцять дру́гого бе́резня.' (On Saturday, March twenty-second.) Ukrainians write a date with the day first and the month second, so 22.03 is March 22.

examples.source: In December there is snow in Kyiv.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: по́друзі, бра́тові, сі́чня and лю́того
grammar.explanation:
Every new word and form in this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. The points below are the ones the dative and the months bring up.

The dative ending '-і' causes the same consonant changes as the locative ending '-і': 'г' becomes 'з', 'к' becomes 'ц' and 'х' becomes 'с'. So 'по́друга' becomes 'по́друзі' [ˈpɔdruzʲi], 'ті́тка' becomes 'ті́тці' and 'жі́нка' becomes 'жі́нці'. The new consonant is soft, as every such consonant is before 'і'. The masculine ending '-ові' begins with 'о', so it changes nothing: 'друг', 'дру́гові'.

'Бра́тові' [ˈbrɑtɔʋi] has three syllables, and the stress stays on the stem, where 'бра́та' has it. Its 'в' stands before a vowel, so it is [ʋ], only slightly softened by the 'і'. The first vowel of the ending shows the kind of stem:

- '-ові' after a hard consonant: 'бра́тові', 'Тара́сові'
- '-еві' after a soft consonant: 'вчи́телеві'
- '-єві' after 'й', because 'й' plus 'е' is written 'є': 'Андрі́єві' [ɑnˈdrʲijɛʋi]

Ten month names end in '-ень': 'сі́чень', 'бе́резень', 'кві́тень', 'тра́вень', 'че́рвень', 'ли́пень', 'се́рпень', 'ве́ресень', 'жо́втень', 'гру́день'. Two rules apply to all of them.

First, the 'е' before the last consonant is there only when the word ends with that consonant. When an ending is added, the 'е' drops out: 'сі́чень', 'сі́чня'; 'гру́день', 'гру́дня'. The same 'е' drops in 'ти́ждень', 'ти́жня', and in 'день', 'дні' ('два дні', two days), and an 'о' drops the same way in 'ри́нок', 'на ри́нку' and in 'пода́рунок', 'пода́рунка'.

Second, the 'н' is soft in every form. At the end of the word the soft sign shows it: 'сі́чень' [ˈsʲit͡ʃɛnʲ]. In the genitive the 'я' shows it, 'сі́чня' [ˈsʲit͡ʃnʲɑ], and in the locative the 'і' does, 'у сі́чні'. The stress stays on the first syllable in every form ('бе́резень', 'бе́резня', 'у бе́резні'), so the unstressed 'е' of 'бе́резень' and 'ве́ресень' leans toward 'и'. 'Жо́втень' has the [w] of 'жо́втий', because its 'в' stands before a consonant.

'Листопа́д' ends in a hard 'д', which stays voiced at the end of the word, [lɪstɔˈpɑd], and its genitive is 'листопа́да'.

'Лю́тий' is a noun with the endings of an adjective, because it was the adjective 'лю́тий', fierce, before it became the name of the month: genitive 'лю́того' [ˈlʲutɔɦɔ], locative 'у лю́тому'. The 'г' of '-ого' is the voiced [ɦ] of every other 'г'. The 'л' is soft before 'ю'.

The other new words:

- 'Наро́дження' [nɑˈrɔd͡ʒɛnʲːɑ]: 'дж' is one sound, and the doubled 'нн' before 'я' is one long soft consonant, as in 'життя́'.
- 'Допомогти́' [dɔpɔmɔxˈtɪ]: before the voiceless 'т', 'г' is said [x], as in 'могти́'. The spelling keeps the 'г' that 'допомага́ти' and 'допомогла́' show.
- 'Подо́бається' and 'подо́баються' end in '-ться', said [t͡sʲːɑ], as in 'прокида́ється'.
- 'Мі́сяць' [ˈmʲisʲɑt͡sʲ] has a soft 'с' before 'я' and a soft 'ць' at the end.
- 'Число́' moves its stress in the plural, 'чи́сла', as 'вікно́' does in 'ві́кна'.
- 'Їй' is [jij]: 'ї' is always [ji], and 'й' follows it.
- 'Дарува́ти' changes '-ува-' to '-у-' in the present, 'дару́ю', like 'купува́ти' and 'купу́ю'.
- 'Здоро́в’я', health, in the culture note: the apostrophe after 'в' keeps the 'в' hard and the [j] sounded, as in 'м’я́со': [zdɔˈrɔʋjɑ].
- 'Ща́стя', happiness, and 'Незале́жності', of independence: the 'т' is soft before 'я' and 'і', and the 'с' before it is said soft as well: [ˈʃt͡ʃɑsʲtʲɑ].
- 'Іва́нівна', in the name 'Марі́я Іва́нівна', has the [w] of 'Петрі́вна', because its 'в' stands before a consonant. Her name in the vocative is 'Марі́є', as 'Со́фія' gives 'Со́фіє'.

examples.source: We are giving our aunt a book.

culture.title: Months named by nature, and birthdays
culture.text:
The English names of the months come from the calendar of ancient Rome: July and August, for example, are named after Julius Caesar and the emperor Augustus. The Ukrainian names come from the farming year and the natural world, so each one says something about its season:

- 'сі́чень', January: from the verb 'сі́кти', to cut, the time when trees were cut
- 'лю́тий', February: fierce, for its hard frosts
- 'бе́резень', March: from 'бере́за', birch, whose sap is gathered in spring
- 'кві́тень', April: from 'квіт', blossom
- 'тра́вень', May: from 'трава́', grass
- 'че́рвень', June: from 'черве́ць', a small insect gathered in this month to make red dye
- 'ли́пень', July: from 'ли́па', the linden tree, which flowers in July
- 'се́рпень', August: from 'серп', the sickle of the harvest
- 'ве́ресень', September: from 'ве́рес', heather
- 'жо́втень', October: from 'жо́втий', yellow, for the leaves
- 'листопа́д', November: falling leaves
- 'гру́день', December: from 'гру́да', a frozen lump of earth

On a birthday, friends and family say 'З днем наро́дження!' and add a wish. The verb 'бажа́ти', to wish, takes the person in the dative and the thing wished in the genitive: 'Бажа́ю тобі́ здоро́в’я й ща́стя!' means 'I wish you health and happiness', literally 'I-wish to-you of-health and of-happiness'. Guests bring a present and often flowers, and a bouquet always has an odd number of flowers, because even numbers are for funerals. At work the person whose birthday it is often brings a cake or sweets for colleagues.

Some dates matter to everyone. On September first, 'День знань', the Day of Knowledge, the school year begins, and children bring flowers to their teachers. August twenty-fourth is 'День Незале́жності', Independence Day, which marks the declaration of independence in 1991. Since 2023 Ukraine has celebrated 'Різдво́', Christmas, on December twenty-fifth.

exercises.prompt: Match the first six months with their English names
Match the last six months with their English names
Match each dative pronoun with its meaning

pairs.source: to you, said to a friend

exercises.prompt: Which question does the dative case answer when it names a person?
exercises.explanation: 'Кому́?' means 'to whom?', the question of the person who receives. 'Кого́?' asks for the genitive or the accusative of a person, and 'де?' asks where.

exercises.prompt: What does the month name 'листопа́д' say word for word?
exercises.explanation: 'Листопа́д' joins 'лист', leaf, and the verb 'па́дати', to fall: November is the month when the leaves fall. The month named for yellow leaves is 'жо́втень'.

exercises.prompt: Which form of 'по́друга' is the dative?
exercises.explanation: Feminine nouns in '-а' take '-і' in the dative, and 'г' becomes 'з' before it: 'по́друзі'. 'По́други' is the genitive and 'по́другу' the accusative.

exercises.prompt: Which ending is preferred in the dative of a man's name such as 'Тара́с'?
exercises.explanation: Masculine nouns take '-ові' or '-у' in the dative, and '-ові' is preferred for people. 'Тара́са' is the genitive and the accusative, and 'Тара́се' is the vocative.
'Хо́лодно' is a predicative word, and the dative 'мені́' names the person who feels the cold. Without 'мені́', as in 'Сього́дні хо́лодно.', the sentence describes the weather.

exercises.hint_source: I am giving Mom a book.
exercises.explanation: Mom receives the book, so she is in the dative: 'ма́ма' becomes 'ма́мі'. The book is the direct object, in the accusative.
'Допомага́ти' takes the person helped in the dative. 'Брат' takes '-ові' or '-у', and '-ові' is preferred for people.
The person helped is in the dative, and the dative of 'ти' is 'тобі́'. 'Тебе́' is the accusative.

exercises.prompt: Which word completes 'Тара́се, ___ подо́бається Ки́їв?' (Taras, do you like Kyiv?)
exercises.explanation: With 'подо́батися' the city is the subject and the person who likes it is in the dative: 'тобі́ подо́бається Ки́їв', literally 'to-you pleases Kyiv'.
The songs are the subject, and 'пі́сні' is plural, so the verb is 'подо́баються'. One song takes 'подо́бається'.

exercises.prompt: Why is the verb 'подо́бається' in 'Мені́ подо́бається ця пі́сня'?
choices: 'Ця пі́сня' is the subject, and the verb agrees with it.
'Мені́' is the subject, and this is its form of the verb.
This verb has only one form.
exercises.explanation: 'Подо́батися' means to please. The song is what pleases, so it is the subject, and the person it pleases is in the dative. With several songs the verb changes to 'подо́баються'.

exercises.hint_source: I will give my sister a dress.
exercises.explanation: 'Сестрі́' is a feminine noun in the dative, and a possessive before it takes the feminine dative ending '-ій': 'мої́й сестрі́'.

exercises.hint_source: Iryna Petrivna, you need to rest.
exercises.explanation: 'Тре́ба' takes the person in the dative. Sam says 'ви' to his teacher, and the dative of 'ви' is 'вам'.

exercises.prompt: In 'Йому́ два́дцять ро́ків.', why is the pronoun 'йому́'?
choices: It is the nominative, because it is the subject.
It is the dative, because it names the person whose age is given.
It is the accusative, because it is the object.
exercises.explanation: Age is given with the person in the dative, literally 'to-him twenty of-years'. The same pattern gives 'Мені́ два́дцять ро́ків.' and 'Скі́льки тобі́ ро́ків?'.

choices: We have a holiday on November twentieth.
We have a holiday on December thirtieth.
We have a holiday on December twentieth.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'on the first of May'?
exercises.explanation: On a date, the ordinal goes into the genitive with no preposition: 'пе́ршого тра́вня'. 'Пе́рше тра́вня' names the date, as in 'Сього́дні пе́рше тра́вня.', and 'у тра́вні' means in May.
In the answer to 'Яке́ сього́дні число́?' the ordinal agrees with the word 'число́', which is left out, so it is neuter: 'пе́рше'.

exercises.hint_source: The holiday will be on August twenty-fourth.
exercises.explanation: On a date, the ordinal is in the genitive. In a compound number only the last word is an ordinal and changes: 'два́дцять четве́ртого'.

exercises.hint_source: We will be at the sea in July.
exercises.explanation: A month without a date takes 'у' or 'в' and the locative. 'Ли́пень' loses its 'е' and takes '-і': 'в ли́пні'.

exercises.prompt: Why is January 'сі́чень', but 'сі́чня' in 'п’я́те сі́чня'?
choices: The 'е' before the last consonant drops out when an ending is added, as in 'ти́ждень', 'ти́жня'.
exercises.explanation: 'Сі́чня' is the genitive singular, the form a month takes after a date. The 'е' of '-ень' drops out before the ending '-я', and the 'н' stays soft.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'у лю́тому' but 'у бе́резні'?
choices: 'Лю́тий' is a noun that keeps the endings of the adjective it comes from.
exercises.explanation: 'Лю́тий' was the adjective fierce before it became the name of the month, so it declines like an adjective: 'лю́того', 'у лю́тому', like 'у вели́кому мі́сті'.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'Я дзвоню́ ма́мі.' have 'ма́мі', where English says 'I'm calling Mom' with no 'to'?
choices: 'Ма́мі' is the subject of the sentence.
'Дзвони́ти' takes the person in the dative, because the call goes to her.
exercises.explanation: 'Дзвони́ти', 'допомага́ти' and 'дя́кувати' take the person in the dative, although English uses a direct object. The accusative of 'ма́ма' is 'ма́му'.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, what will Oksana and Taras give Olena for her birthday?
exercises.explanation: Taras gave her a book last year. Oksana suggests 'квитки́ на конце́рт', and they will buy them together.

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, on what date is Iryna Petrivna's birthday?
exercises.explanation: Sam phones on her birthday, and she says 'Сього́дні два́дцять дру́ге.' Independence Day, two days later, is August twenty-fourth.

exercises.prompt: In the third dialogue, what does Andrii tell Mariia Ivanivna she needs to do?
choices: Go to the post office today
exercises.explanation: Andrii says 'Вам тре́ба сього́дні йти на по́шту', so that the present will be in Lviv tomorrow. The cup is his present.

exercises.prompt_source: I need to go to the post office.

exercises.explanation: The city is the subject of 'подо́батися', and the person who likes it is in the dative.
'Тре́ба' takes the person in the dative, 'Тара́сові' or 'Тара́су', and an infinitive.

exercises.prompt_source: Today is the third of October.
exercises.explanation: The ordinal is neuter, agreeing with the word 'число́' that is left out, and the month is in the genitive.

'Допомогти́' takes the person in the dative, and 'допоможу́' is its perfective future, for one act of help. The imperfective future, 'бу́ду допомага́ти' or 'допомага́тиму', is also correct for help that goes on or is repeated.
